translation: Aristotle, and likewise Theophrastus too, have stated precisely what one must look to in order to suppose a nature to be well-tempered or of bad temperament; but these people do not even know this. Rather, when they hear them saying that the animal is moist and warm, or that the mixture of the child is moist and warm, they neither understand how these things are said, and they recklessly transfer the account to the seasons, as though it were the same thing, or not far different, for one's own mixture to be moist and warm and for that of the air surrounding us to be so. For it is neither the same thing, nor is a moist and warm mixture of an animal so called in the same way as a moist and warm mixture of air. What, then, was the cause of all these things I shall now explain, and I shall show clearly to those willing to pay attention how small slips in the

the same, or to evacuate a moisture of something dispersed in certain spaces, or to render its own mixture drier. For an uneven bad temperament arises in inflamed parts, the homoeomerous bodies not yet having departed from their own nature but still being changed and altered, while all the spaces between them are filled with the flux. All things, then, that are warm and moist in mixture, when applied to parts so disposed, evacuate that superfluity which has occupied the spaces between the homoeomerous bodies, but are so far from drying the bodies themselves that they even add moisture to them. This, then, is how the truth stands; but what has been said requires a demonstration, which, since I consider it too long to be added in this treatise, and moreover as requiring a hearer acquainted with the power of drugs, I postpone; at least

at least, and with rose cerate it benefits greatly; for which, indeed, and for such conditions, many other drugs too will be described in the following discussion, some having a power similar to the palm plaster, some even more active. But for conditions subject to a discharge or flux this drug is the best of all, and has often achieved something beyond hope. Once, then, when a thigh had suppurated near the groin, the inflammation throughout the whole of it being unconcocted, the leg was positioned by us so that the ichors flowed out towards the groin through the wound that had been made; and when this had gone on for a longer time, the flux that had descended into the thigh was evacuated, but a fistulous condition arose under the skin throughout the whole thigh, so that I wished to incise it near the kneecap, in order that on either side there might be an outflow for the ichors

about nourishment, since the bad and the not-bad, and evidently also the harmful and the beneficial, are spoken of in the category of relation. For in another sense you might say that the Attalic is better than this plaster, in that that one is of more extensive use. Indeed Asclepiades himself, writing next after this one now mentioned that very one with white pepper, does not name it Attalic but Pamphilian, being ignorant, I think, of the man who first discovered it, and adding the name of the one who used it and gave it to him. Its promise, then, he wrote word for word as follows: ‘Another, called Pamphilian, a successful drug; it acts for old and hard-to-heal [lesions], carbuncles, night pustules, achores, conditions of the nature of the itch; it glues down sinuses; it acts for abscesses, condylomata; and the drug is of almost more extensive use.’ And he says it is composed of white lead

each of these precisely, for the sake of contributing something to the whiteness of the drug. Concerning white lead, too, it has been said before, and concerning the oil, the manner of boiling, the surrounding air and the fire, how each of them may contribute something to the whiteness. And just as in the other cases, so in these too one must, knowing the powers of water, vinegar, seawater and the whitest wine, mix into the composition what is most useful for the condition being treated. For in the case of callous ulcers, which have lips thick and hard and in need of much thinning, the ingredients triturated with vinegar and seawater are more useful than those triturated with water; but in those in which the moisture carried in the ulcers is acrid and biting, one should rather have triturated them in water

each of the metallic ingredients, just as, again, rather in wine in those in which the moisture flowing onto the ulcers appears copious. Having, then, put each of those I mentioned, triturated in each of the said liquids for several days, each time into the drugs made with white lead and litharge, I tested them all, and they cicatrize excellently; and I gave some of the formulas to friends who needed such drugs, and when put to the trial by them too they were seen to keep their promise. So, the litharge having been boiled beforehand with the white lead, as has been said, and the drug having come close to a non-soiling consistency, one must add some of the larch or terebinth resin of the pine together with the white wax, and when these have been well united, add in the metallic ingredients, having the following proportion: of the litharge and the white lead, as usual, a litra of each, let it be boiled with two litrai of oil, often

but if something of its inflammation should remain scirrhous, to apply one of those that dry sufficiently. Since, then, something seemed to be lacking in the drug made with the root of dragonwort, which I used first, which in other respects has the same ingredients as the Egyptian drug called Isis but has taken in addition the root of dragonwort, and having next after this used the one called Athena, from that one I then went on to the cicatrizing drugs. In another case, smearing the bared parts of the wound with the pastille dissolved in boiled-down must, I laid the euphorbium on the outside, mixing it with wax and resin of the pine in such quantity that it both became plaster-like and preserved the power of the euphorbium. How one might compose the drug looking to these aims I shall say next; for indeed I also made another drug with vinegar

just as with the resin of the pine and the pitch. For this reason I mix into the cerate resin of the pine or pitch, or a portion of each. It is quite clear, then, that when these are mixed in, the oil is no longer to be put in equal to them; for wax needs much fat for moistness, while of the resins of the pine the wholly dry ones require little, and the moist ones even want to take in some dry substance in addition to reach a plaster-like consistency. Among waxes, then, the difference in moistness and dryness is not great, but with the resins of the pine, conversely, as also with pitch, the difference of the dry ones from the moist ones is very great. The driest of the resins of the pine, then, is the one which some call roasted and others Colophonian; second is the one from the potteries, unpurified and unroasted; but if one purifies it

you have seen me doing constantly, not only with this but also with the ammoniac incense. There is also the drug written next by the Tarentine, of the same promise, in this proportion: of chalcitis 25 drachms, of cadmia 12 drachms; having triturated them separately and mixed them, boil unmixed wine and pour it over so that it is kneaded moderately; then triturate until it is dried; and having melted wax 50 drachms, terebinth resin of the pine 30 drachms, myrtle oil 8 kotylai, mix into the cerate 20 drachms of the dry ingredients. This drug too has nothing of the softening ones; in mixing it with the cerate, however, one trained methodically in the methods I set out would suitably work out the quantity of the mixture appropriate for each of the ulcers. And well too [is used] the unmixed wine, that is, that with which seawater has not been mixed

the meltables, having let them cool somewhat, sprinkle the dry ingredients onto them, stirring carefully. One must have ready, triturated with vinegar, myrrh, frankincense, bdellium, opopanax; and into these the contents of the dish are put and triturated so that lumps of wax do not form. When it is in good condition, take it up into a wooden box, having first smeared it with iris oil. On the third class of hard-to-cure ulcers, about which Asclepiades wrote word for word as follows: ‘In the case of ulcers that do not close at all, or that close but break open again, either because the flesh is being corrupted or because the underlying bones are decayed, one must use the preparations set out below. For chironian and hard-to-heal ulcers, a successful drug: of copper flake and scraped verdigris, 1 ounce each; of wax half a litra; of larch resin of the pine 1½ ounces; [pour] the meltables over the dry ingredients and, taking it up, use it, softening it carefully and throwing a small spread plaster over

the metallic ingredients with vinegar, and after this adding the dry ingredients and triturating again; then, when these have a mud-like consistency, mixing in the meltables, as said before. Another: of asphalt, terebinth resin of the pine and Bruttian pitch, 1 litra each; of oil 24 drachms; of litharge, white lead, frankincense powder, verdigris, flake and opopanax, of each an amount equal to the twenty-four drachms of the oil; of ladanum two ounces, which is 16 drachms; and two kotylai of vinegar. This drug too is prepared in the same way as the two before it. Another: of chrysocolla, flake and steel, 4 drachms each; of verdigris and copper vitriol half of each, that is 2 drachms each; of wax 25 drachms, that is 3 ounces and one drachm; of terebinth resin of the pine 2 ounces, that is 16 drachms. Melt the wax with the terebinth

Of rust of copper and Indian aloe, of burnt copper and good diphryges, sixteen and a half of each for the mixture; twenty drachms of the resinous juice of all-heal, and 4; of frankincense powder the same, twice 12; of ammoniac twice 5 and twice 20; sixteen drachms of Attic propolis; of long birthwort twice 10 drachms; twice 6 drachms of flake of Cyprian copper; and of the driest gentian root an equal amount. To all these add of the herb of dittany, dry and in flower, 20 holkai, finely ground. Putting litharge with oil into a new, wide-mouthed earthenware dish, boil it on a light and gentle fire, stirring with a spatula, until it reaches the thickness of Attic honey; and adding again an equal amount of the flake, boil it more vigorously; then, when the drug has become tawny, add the copper and the diphryges, making the drug non-soiling and set; add the wax and the

of wax, having neither of these, but the ammoniac incense alone, put in, will make the drug parched. But for plaster-making (for it is not bad to name it so) both the wax and the resin of the pine are useful; for softening and dispersing belong to the drug from the ammoniac alone, which is foremost among the emollients and a match for the discutients as well. If you recall what was said in the fifth book of On the Power of Simple Drugs, of what sort the mixture must be in such drugs, you will need no further teaching. For the primary active powers in drugs lie in heat, cold, moisture and dryness; the secondary are the emollient, discutient, repellent, attractive, concoctive, detergent and septic, just as also

all of it carefully; again let a little drip off; and if you see it of good colour and well blended, take the pot off the fire at once, and add the resinous juice of all-heal, softened beforehand. But if the drug is much too hard, add oil to it to bring it to a good blend. Then, straining it thus into another vessel, soften it cold with the hands and so store it away. I shall write out another, of the same kind as the one before this. It acts for the affections I mentioned earlier; better than all drugs this one cicatrizes ulcers hard to heal, callous and chronic; the eruptions arising on the face this one treats without any bad biting; and seats that have fissures and hardnesses; the condylomatous growths and calluses it removes. Prepare it thus: a mina of good litharge (a mina is a litra and a third part of a litra); of good Pontic wax half a mina; of verdigris a fourth part of a mina, good, scraped

scrofulous swellings; reducing every oedema, and healing the watery conditions of the liver or spleen; bringing on copious discharges of urine; and it resolves chronic sciaticas. Using this, Ulpianus, a gifted young man, benefited very many people. It contains one litra of Pontic wax, one of roasted [resin] and one of the pine [resin], of fresh quicklime 1 ounce, of split alum 1 ounce, and of Pontic orpiment an amount equal to one of these. Pouring a little fragrant vinegar over these, triturate sufficiently in a larger mortar; adding a little oil to the wax and the resin of the pine, melting it over a fire of fierce flame, mixing everything carefully, and making it into malagmata, bringing it to the thickness of a non-soiling drug, keep it in store. Use it, where needed, on a fresh compress. Kratistos, the father of the drug, said also that for the relief of long diseases

which also heal the small inflammations. Of the compound emollients, some are, as one might say, weaker, in the first order; some not much stronger than these, in the second; and some in the third, and others besides these in the fourth. One should use, as was said before, for slight hardnesses and soft bodies those of the first order; for those stronger than these, both bodies and affections, those of the second, just as also those of the third and of the fourth proportionally. They also describe those in each of them separately. Emollient drugs of the first order: butter, or Colophonian resin of the pine, and white wax not old, equal in weight, the 3 melted together, are emollient of the first order; and so is the parygros, when it is fresh.
